en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
In the *Nītimañjarī*:
When a family perishes, they are destroyed.
The family traditions are eternal;
when the Dhamma is lost, the entire family is overcome by unrighteousness and becomes base.
Women with skin are corrupted by the overwhelming power of unrighteousness; when women are corrupted,
they [corrupt] their own nature.
There arises a confusion of castes.
One should speak kindly, appreciate virtues,
be courageous, and be decisive.
A woman who gives like the moon makes one smile at every sight.
Where can there be truth among bad friends?
In a bad wife, the increase of passion;
in a bad country, a delightful mind;
in a bad kingdom, the perfection of enjoyments.
There is no difference between an enemy and a friend;
from one who was once fearless, fear may arise.
He even cuts down the roots.
Better is the stranger who has not seen you than a bad friend who is trustworthy.
The fruit of the Veda is the fire-sacrifice;
the fruit of the Teacher is considered to be virtue;
the fruit of a woman is pleasure and sons.
The fruit of giving is wealth.
Untruth, recklessness, deceit,
delusion, and excessive greed;
Sorrow, cruelty, and sloth—
these faults are inherent in her nature.
It is the husband’s burden regarding his wife.
The pupil did it for the teacher;
the ministers did it for the king;
and parents did it for their own children.
For deeds are accomplished through exertion, not by mere wishes;
for a sleeping lion, indeed, [does not catch his prey].
Deer enter into his mouth.
This has become too cold, too hot, and too late.
Thus, for a person whose actions are neglected,
the opportune moments pass by.
Of grasping and of giving...
And for a task that ought to be done,
if it is not performed quickly,
one drinks failure even at the time of success.
No action whatsoever,
even with a hundredfold effort, will bear fruit if it is placed upon a non-existent object.
The crane recites the verse:
"He who is slow when he ought to cross,
and crosses quickly when he ought to be slow;"
Like crushing a dry leaf,
he destroys his own welfare—
whatever he gives and whatever he enjoys.
That alone is the wealth of the wealthy;
others sport with the wife and the riches of the deceased.
What difference is there between a wealthy man who possesses wealth devoid of both giving and enjoyment, and a pauper?
Excessive guarding of wealth,
obstructing one's own happiness, lowly enjoyments,
and eating only a little.
He who accumulates wealth is a beast that carries the burden of another;
he for whom they labor with eager effort—
One who lacks fortune does not enjoy much wealth;
whether one possesses a craft or is without a craft,
it is fortune that enjoys those things.
The mind of the great, when rising,
is like a tender lotus; yet when falling,
it is like a massive rock.
Having heard of his inconceivable qualities,
weariness arises in vain, as if toward a harsh mass of stone.
Having looked at the moon, one does not say,
"It is not the moon"; one should maintain the truth within one's mouth.
In his ear, he heard victory;
in his heart, the patient hero;
and in his eyes, the light of the world.
One would not tremble with pride,
having understood the cause of sound; by fully comprehending the reason for faith, one does not waver.
Or through negligence or fear, one might forget all that has been heard—
the inferior, the superior, and the middling.
A low-born man enters a pure family,
yet the son perishes through indulgence;
O Samiddhi, such is the ruin brought by a kinsman.
She was intoxicated by her stay abroad and devoid of shame;
she cooed for five years and struck me for ten.
When he has reached his sixteenth year,
one should treat a son like a friend.
There are many faults in pampering him.
There are many virtues in nurturing:
one wards off evil, joins others with what is beneficial,
conceals secrets, and makes virtues manifest.
The virtuous declare that one who does not abandon an offense but confesses it at the proper time possesses the characteristic of a true friend.
Through reasoned argument, the wicked man is defeated.
By one lacking wisdom,
even with suppression, the great tree is felled by the exhaustion of the roots dug near it.
In the forest, deer are enemies of hunters,
and the virtuous are enemies of the wicked;
they are foes without cause.
Those who subsist on grass are very gentle;
they remove what is stuck to their feet with their own hooves,
just as one removes a thorn with another thorn.
One should not see a fool, nor hear one,
nor dwell together with a fool;
one should avoid conversation and discourse with a fool.
One should not act for one's own pleasure;
just as a small person is capable of doing something,
a great person is not capable of that same thing.
For a well indeed quenches thirst,
but not the great ocean,
which is a place for taking up and giving away.
But for one who does not quickly perform the deed that ought to be done,
Time devours that very essence.
While waiting for the auspicious moment,
profit came to the fool;
profit is the auspicious moment for profit.
What can the stars do?
One who is wise and free from old age and death should contemplate true knowledge and the ultimate goal.
Even when seized by the hair by Death,
one should practice the Dhamma;
one should honor both teachers and counselors.
There are three types of royal administration:
the skillful management of livelihoods,
the increase of treasuries, and their depletion.
By steadiness, work prospers;
by unsteadiness, it does not.
Trees bear fruit in due season.
Even though one is drenched by much water,
a person should still exert effort;
a wise person should not lose heart.
Such exertion is not at all appropriate for one by whom no fruit is attained;
it is like digging a well on the peak of a mountain.
How is there a meeting with the waters?
The elephant of exertion for deliverance follows the right path by means of the goad of knowledge.
The deeds that burn those who have acted without reflection and who fall headlong into haste—
those very deeds torment them.
Just as hot food swallowed into the mouth must be spat out,
so too should these six faults be abandoned by a man who desires prosperity in this world.
Sleep, intoxication, fear, anger,
laziness, and prolixity— these are not found in one of virtuous conduct who does not sleep by day.
By one who wakes at night,
who is constantly sober and not intoxicated,
it is possible to dwell at home.
They fear what is not to be feared,
and they do not fear what is to be feared; those who are confused about fear and fearlessness, [are lost].
One who follows crookedness and abandons the straight path—
such a person, while having been born as a human,
possesses neither wealth nor craft.
What fruit is there for him in being human?
For he is but a two-legged beast. One must employ various means.
If one were to possess one's own means for accomplishing one’s welfare as desired,
then that method would indeed be effective for achieving benefit.
By means of bribery, gifts,
and tribute, the fraudulent tax-collectors and fishermen [caught] the great fish of the legal decision.
They wallow in the ocean of greed.
He in whom these four qualities exist,
O Lord of Monkeys, just as they do in you;
Truth, Dharma, steadfastness, and generosity—
he transcends what is seen.
The wise man is a jewel, a woman.
The lute makes its voice meaningful by attaining excellence of qualities;
it reveals both virtues and faults.
In this world, one who has wealth is powerful;
through wealth, one becomes wise.
A worm that relies on a jasmine flower—
Even one who is devoid of virtues and base by nature—
by adorning such a person with flowers,
even the head of kings grows weary.
Wealth and enjoyments accumulated by those who lack fortune,
though they were intended for them,
become theirs only when they possess fortune.
Lakkhi indeed enjoys well.
Among those who rely on lineage, the khattiya is the best among people.
One endowed with true knowledge and conduct is the best among gods and humans;
even from poison, one may take the deathless.
A supreme jewel from dung;
a flower from a thorny tree;
and fine cloth from coarse rags.
I am one whose qualities such as sovereignty over wealth have been swiftly carried away;
yet for him who possesses constant loving-kindness, there is no loss.
Beloved by the entire world,
even the ocean acts like a well,
and fire acts like water for him.
Even Mount Meru seems like a grain of sugar;
one who eats filth seems like nectar;
and the king of beasts seems like a hare.
The tiger acts like a string of garlands;
the earth-dweller swings like a swing;
various weapons are like blades of grass.
When there is such effort,
it brings happiness and accomplishes what is beneficial;
likewise, let there be neither deficiency nor excess.
It is always good to be moderate;
indeed, it is good to be wise,
but not to be excessively wise.
